L27: ## Cultural Heritage and Identity Formation: A Study of Second-Generation Immigrant Children through Parental Perspectives in Singapore
L28: 
L29: 【10†Yi Fei LOH  】
L30: 【11†Lee Tat CHOW 】
L31: 【12†Peidong YANG 】
L32: 
L33: 
L34: 
L35: Keywords
L36: identity
L37: immigrant
L38: education
L39: ethnic cultures
L40: 
L41: Abstract
L42: This paper explores how immigrant parents influence the development of their children’s identities in Singapore, drawing on qualitative interviews with parents from diverse backgrounds. A key focus is the balance between maintaining ethnic traditions and integrating into Singapore society, along with parents’ aspirations for their children’s national identity.
L43: It is found that immigrant parents play an active role in transmitting heritage cultural values and practices to their children, with a focus on maintaining a connection to their heritage while also promoting societal integration into the host country. This approach is particularly reflected in the parents’ discourse about their children’s linguistic maintenance and adaptation.
L44: This research adds more broadly to the understanding of the immigrant experience and its implications for social cohesion and multiculturalism in Singapore.

The struggles of single parenthood - CNA (https://www.channelnewsasia.com/cna-insider/big-read/single-parents-unwed-divorced-challenges-support-5465031)
【turn633889view4】 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: today; Content type: text/html; Source: find({"ref_id":"https://www.channelnewsasia.com/cna-insider/big-read/single-parents-unwed-divorced-challenges-support-5465031","pattern":"58 per cent"}); Total lines: 250
L64: ###### 【15†‘I don’t want to give up on love’: Dating after divorce and how self-healing helps women overcome fear】
L65: 
L66: Because of such differentiated policies, unwed single mothers are among the most structurally disadvantaged in society, especially if they are also from low-income groups, according to family and social policy experts.
L67: 
L68: Strides have been made to better support solo parents, but interviews with seven of them reflect the many challenges that remain.
L69: An average of about 745 children annually were born to unwed Singaporean mothers between 2020 and 2024, revealed Minister for Social and Family Development Masagos Zulkifli in a written parliamentary reply last month.
L70: This already small figure – comparable to less than 3 per cent of resident live births last year – reflects a declining trend in roughly the past two decades. The average number of children born out of wedlock was 830 per year between 2016 and 2020, a dip from more than 1,000 annually from 2006 to 2012.
L71: The overall number of lone parent resident households – which includes divorced or widowed parents – declined in terms of proportion of total number of resident households, from about 6.84 per cent in 2005 to 5.06 per cent last year.
L72: 
L73: Relatively small though the population of single parents may be, there has been some progress over time in extending support to this group, observed single parents and experts alike.
L74: As a baseline, benefits such as subsidies for education, healthcare, childcare and infant care as well as the migrant domestic helper levy concession, are extended to parents regardless of their marital status.
L75: 
L76: More recent moves to support solo parents include the removal of a wait-out period to buy a house after a divorce, extending maternal leave as well as a savings scheme with government co-matching funding to children born to unwed mothers.
L77: Nonetheless, the experts and parents whom CNA TODAY spoke to pointed to persistent gaps in the system. These disparities exist partly because many family-related policies are differentiated to align with the longstanding official position of promoting parenthood specifically in marriages.
L78: 
L79: “Many public supports, particularly in housing and family schemes, were designed with traditional family nuclei in mind," said Ms Kaylee Kua, executive director of Daughters of Tomorrow.
L80: "This means that unwed single parents or those who’ve recently separated can find themselves navigating eligibility gaps that affect housing, childcare and income stability."
L81: 
L82: If left unaddressed, such gaps may have repercussions for the well-being of the single parents and result in long-term effects on their children, the experts noted.
L122: 【20†Image†dam.mediacorp.sg】 The number of lone parent resident households has declined, in terms of proportion of total number of resident households, from about 6.84 per cent in 2005 to 5.06 per cent last year. (Photo: iStock)
L123: ## WOES OF "SINGLE-AGAIN" PARENTS
L124: 
L125: While single parents who were previously married may have better policy support than unwed ones, they continue to face other challenges.
L126: 
L127: These include legal disputes, emotional trauma and the financial strain of running a single-income household.
L128: 
L129: Ms Sophia Evangel Cheah can attest to that, with the 45-year-old still dealing with fallout from her acrimonious divorce back in 2020.
L172: Ms Vivian Pan, a single mother of a 20-year-old son, who runs an informal support group for single parents, feels that society in general has also become more empathetic towards single parents.
L173: 
L174: She recalled how in 2013, when news broke about a single mother with a mental illness who had fatally pushed her child out of her window, it was met with intense public criticism and contempt, with some accusing single parents in general of being irresponsible and bad parents.
L175: The tragedy prompted Ms Pan to create a support group, which in its early years organised events to encourage single parent families to socialise and find support in one another. Ms Pan now focuses on providing advice and emotional support to parents who approach her.
L176: 
L177: "Today, I think the stigma is a lot less. More people are willing to talk about their situation as single parents and about divorce, and so are more willing to reach out for help," said Ms Pan, 45.
L178: 【23†Image†dam.mediacorp.sg】 Ms Vivian Pan is a single mother to a 20-year-old son. (Photo: CNA/Alyssa Tan)
L179: 
L180: 【24†Image†dam.mediacorp.sg】 Ms Vivian Pan, who runs an informal support group for single parents, says society has also become more empathetic towards them.(Photo: CNA/Alyssa Tan)
L181: ## THE CASE FOR SUPPORTING SINGLE PARENTS
L182: 
L183: If policies towards single parents are indeed partly shaped by prevailing societal views, it is noteworthy that attitudes, specifically towards having children out of wedlock, are liberalising, according to some research.
L184: 
L185: A 2024 survey conducted by IPS found 58 per cent of respondents disapproved of pregnancy outside of marriage, down from 64.9 per cent in 2019 and 73.5 per cent in 2013.
L186: A separate, one-off survey that same year by non-profit group Cultivate also found 83 per cent polled believed that single parents should receive more support.
L187: 
L188: More importantly, experts said, providing equal support to such families and their children means ensuring that they are not unnecessarily placed at a disadvantage that could affect the course of their lives in the long term.
L189: Assistant Professor Yong Ming Lee from the National Institute of Education said that circumstances in a single-parent household, if left unchecked, could impact the children’s long-term development.
L190: 
L191: For starters, due to the likelihood of the household having a lower income with just one parent working, it might limit the children’s access to quality childcare and educational support.
L192: "Young children need to experience a positive attachment relationship with a consistent and caring adult, and this is critical and essential for long-term healthy socio-emotional development," she said, adding that such opportunities may be limited with only one parent around.
L193: 
L194: And due to the long-term implications of potentially negative child development outcomes, it is important to proactively provide preventative social services for single-parent households, she added.
L195: Dr Mathew Mathews from IPS said that improving support for single parents here "is really necessary, especially given our desire to remove as many disadvantages as possible for children".
L196: "Given that our total fertility rate in Singapore is dismally low, and many couples who could have children find it hard to and so choose not to, it is hard to imagine how ensuring better support for single parent families will incentivise them to have more children, or for singles to try parenthood outside marriage," he said.
L197: 
L198: Agreeing, Ms Lin of HCSA SPIN said that global studies have shown that marriage and childbirth are deeply personal choices and are usually not driven by social assistance.
L199: And while prioritisation of resources may be necessary in terms of policy, it should not lead to the exclusion of single-parent families who often represent some of the most vulnerable households, she added.
L200: 
L201: "The intent of support is not to encourage single parenthood but to mitigate hardship for children who are already here. This balanced approach strengthens social cohesion and reflects our shared responsibility to ensure that no child is left behind,” Ms Lin said.

L294: # Trust between racial groups in Singapore grows, but stereotyping rises: IPS-OnePeople.sg survey
L295: 
L296: Survey results found that 43.5 per cent of respondents in 2024 said they form assumptions about someone’s behaviour based on their race, up from 35.2 per cent in 2018.
L297:

L299:

L313: OnePeople.sg was first launched by then-Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong in 2007 as an organisation that champions racial harmony initiatives in Singapore.
L314: 
L315: The latest findings from the IPS-OnePeople.sg Indicators of Racial and Religious Harmony study released on Monday (Feb 3) showed that more than three-quarters or 77.6 per cent of respondents trusted over half of Chinese in Singapore to help them during a national crisis like the COVID-19 pandemic.
L316: 
L317: 【74†Image: chart visualization†public.flourish.studio】
L318: About two-thirds of respondents trusted more than half of Malays, Indians, and Eurasians to do the same.

L327: 
L328: This was an improvement from the previous studies in 2013 and 2018, said the survey report.
L329: Meanwhile, the proportion of respondents expressing distrust in other racial groups decreased from 42.7 per cent in 2013 to 27.2 per cent in 2024, with similar trends observed for religious groups.
L330: 
L331: But while the downward trend was "encouraging", there remains room for improvement as over a quarter of Singapore residents still indicate distrust in more than half of other racial groups, said the report.
L332: The third edition of the IPS-OnePeople.sg survey, conducted between April 2024 and August 2024, polled a nationally representative sample of 4,000 Singapore residents aged 18 and above.
L333: 
L334: The survey compares trends across the waves - distinct periods of time in which survey answers were collected from respondents - wherever possible, across 10 indicators of racial and religious harmony such as inter-racial trust and social cohesion.
L335: "These indicators allow us to compare shifts in attitudes and perceptions over time, providing a clearer picture of Singapore’s progress in maintaining harmony and inclusivity," said the report.
L336: ###### 【80†Maintaining racial, religious harmony requires constant attention and effort: Shanmugam】
L337: ###### 【81†Why we need to engage in conversations about race】
L338: 
L339: About seven in 10 survey respondents also agreed or strongly agreed that they do not let a person’s race influence their social interactions - a slight increase compared to previous studies.
L340: 
L341: Despite this, there was also a rise in racial stereotyping, with 43.5 per cent agreeing or strongly agreeing that they form assumptions about someone’s behaviour based on their race.
L342: 
L343: 【82†Image: chart visualization†public.flourish.studio】
L344: This was up from 35.2 per cent in 2018. Racial minorities, along with older, less educated, and less affluent respondents, were more likely to engage in stereotyping, the study noted.
L345: 
L346: One possible reason for this could be internal biases that people have, where one makes assumptions about others such as based on their age or the way they dress, said chairman of OnePeople.sg Janil Puthucheary during a press conference about the survey findings on Monday.
L347: Hence, one way to interpret the data would be that there was an increase in awareness with people becoming "a bit more self-honest" about the assumptions they form when they meet someone, said Dr Puthucheary, who is also senior minister of state for digital development and information, and health.
L348: 
L349: "This is not automatically that the assumption is negative," he said, adding that part of the work done by OnePeople.sg is to educate and engage people on the fact that they do have internal biases.
L350: "It's important to recognise that in ourselves so that we can overcome them and behave in a culturally and socially appropriate way … If you want to say 'regardless of race, language and religion', we have to understand what our internal biases are so that we can overcome them and then behave properly."
L351: ## WORKPLACE DISCRIMINATION
L352: 
L353: In terms of job evaluations, a majority (63.9 per cent) agreed or strongly agreed that race or religion should not be considered, marking a slight increase from 2018 (62 per cent).
L354: 
L355: Respondents also reported that experiences of discrimination at the workplace have decreased, with 7 per cent indicating that they faced discrimination when applying for jobs or during a job promotion process in 2024, compared to 9.3 per cent in 2018.
L356: While on a decline, the study found that workplace discrimination does still affect racial minorities disproportionally.
L357: 
L358: Among those who reported discrimination at work, 57.7 per cent felt that the language used by others excluded them from conversations.
L359: Perceived exclusionary behaviour during job promotions was also another common form of discrimination reported, with 47.7 per cent of respondents perceiving that people from other races were being promoted because of their race, and not their qualifications.
L360: 
L361: In particular, 18.4 per cent of Malay respondents and 16.7 per cent of Indians in 2024 reported feeling racially discriminated against in a job or a job promotion.
L362: This was however a drop from more than a quarter for both Malays and Indians in 2018.
L363: 
L364: Meanwhile, 3.7 per cent of Chinese respondents in 2024 felt the same way, a dip from the 4.1 per cent in 2018.
L365: 
L366: Overall, Chinese respondents were most likely to indicate that they had not felt racially discriminated against regarding a job or a job promotion.
L367: ###### 【83†Singapore passes landmark anti-discrimination Bill for workers】
L368: ###### 【84†Commentary: Do we need a law to remind us of basic workplace decency?】
L369: 
L370: When it comes to selecting employees however, respondents overwhelmingly prioritised ability. Race and religion were seen as not or rarely important by more than six in 10 (62.3 per cent) and seven in 10 (72.3 per cent) respondents respectively.
L371: The majority of respondents also felt there were no significant differences in the effort required by various racial groups to achieve a basic, decent life in Singapore, or to reach top positions in companies.
L372: 
L373: However, about 18 per cent of Malays and Indians felt that they had to work harder or much more than others to have a basic, decent life.
L374: 
L375: Meanwhile, 25.7 per cent of Malay and 21.7 per cent of Indian respondents felt this was also the case to reach top positions.
L376: The survey noted however that these proportions had decreased marginally, ranging from a 2.7 per cent to 6.2 per cent decline, since 2018.
L377: 
L378: Differences were also observed across age, race, and education levels.
L379: 
L380: Older respondents were more likely to believe that people of all races work equally hard to achieve these goals, while younger respondents aged 18 to 35 felt that, in general, Singaporean Chinese and Eurasians need to put in less effort, and Singaporean Malays and Indians need to work harder.
L381: The reason for the latter could be due to individuals being prone to unconscious biases, said the head of IPS social lab and principal research fellow Mathew Mathews.
L382: 
L383: "It's more of a recognition about the fact that there are barriers, more discussion today which is accessed by younger people about discrimination, about what goes on."
L384: 
L385: People are becoming "more and more aware" about those issues compared to those who are older, Dr Mathews added.
L386: ###### 【85†Challenges abound in tackling casual racism in Singapore society】
L387: 
L388: ###### 【86†Commentary: Don’t underestimate casual racism at Singapore workplaces】
L389: ## HIGH LEVEL OF RACIAL AND RELIGIOUS HARMONY
L390: 
L391: The latest report found that two-thirds (65.4 per cent) of respondents in 2024 rated Singapore's racial and religious harmony as high or very high - up from 57.1 per cent in 2018.
L392: 
L393: At the same time, racial minorities were more likely to indicate that racial and religious harmony was at moderate levels. Older respondents were also more likely to indicate high or very high levels compared to those who were younger.
L394: Similar to previous studies, racial and religious acceptance remained the highest for public relationships such as colleague or neighbour, compared to personal relationships like sibling-in-law or spouse.
L395: 
L396: When asked, 78.2 per cent of respondents indicated that they would accept a local-born Chinese as their sibling-in-law. In comparison, 62.1 per cent of those surveyed said they would accept a local-born Malay, and 62.4 per cent a local-born Indian.
L397: In contrast, more respondents said they would accept a local-born Chinese (94.4 per cent), a local-born Malay (91.3 per cent), and a local-born Indian (90.3 per cent) as a colleague.
L398: 
L399: Nevertheless, the racial and religious acceptance for all groups, including new citizens, in public and private relationships had increased over the three studies, IPS noted.
L400: ###### 【87†Singapore tables racial harmony law with powers to invoke restraining orders, community remedial actions】
L401: 
L402: At the same time, just over half of those (53.2 per cent) said they have at least one close friend of another race.
L403: 
L404: While this is a significant increase from a decade ago (45.6 per cent), there was a marginal decrease compared to 2018 (55.5 per cent).
L405: 
L406: The decline could be attributed to an overall decline in close friends, the report noted.
L407: 【88†Image: chart visualization†public.flourish.studio】
L408: 
L409: Regardless of race, the average number of close friends in 2024 was 6.49, a decrease from 10.67 in 2018 and 8.33 in 2013, as reported by respondents.
L410: 
L411: Chinese respondents were significantly less likely to report having at least one close friend of another race (45.3 per cent), compared to their minority-race peers - 72.5 per cent of Malays, 84.5 per cent of Indians, and 85.1 per cent of "Others" respondents.
L412: "This is most likely due to demographics of the population, with minorities much more likely to encounter and subsequently build friendships with majority race persons," the report said.
L413: 
L414: Younger respondents and HDB-dwellers were more likely to report cross-racial friendships compared to their older and private property-dwelling counterparts.
L415: The shift in the number of cross-racial friendships was "unexpected", said Dr Puthucheary. He added that such friendships are important to Singapore's approach in maintaining social cohesion, integration, peace and harmony across society.
L416: 
L417: He pointed out that while more people are open to cross-racial friendships, shrinking social circles means less opportunities to form and strengthen such friendships.
L418: "This is not a Singaporean issue, not just a Singapore issue. Many countries face similar trends. We have to think very carefully about how to address this challenge."
L419: ## TENSIONS
L420: 
L421: Majority of respondents in 2024 felt that Singapore is free from racial and religious tensions.
L422: 
L423: More than eight in 10 agreed that they do not experience such tensions in their daily lives. Older respondents and those with lower educational qualifications were more likely to hold these positive views, the report found.
L424: More than three-quarters of respondents aged above 65 also said they never felt upset because someone insulted their race or racial customs. This was higher than the 42.3 per cent reported for those aged 18 to 35 years old.
L425: 
L426: Chinese respondents were also more likely to say they have never felt upset in the past year by racial insults, than minority-race respondents.
L427: However, certain religious practices, such as the burning of religious items and loud events at void decks, "continue to irritate" 13.7 per cent and 10.1 per cent of respondents respectively in 2024, the report said.
L428: 
L429: This is compared to the 16 per cent for burning of religious items and 9.3 per cent for loud events reported in 2018.
L430: 
L431: While some cultural practices remain as matters of tension, 71.1 per cent of respondents agreed or strongly agreed that racial diversity is beneficial for Singapore.
L432: This was a 4.4 per cent increase from 2018, with Malay and Indian respondents being more likely to value diversity than their Chinese counterparts.
L433: 
L434: Younger respondents were also more likely to express a strong belief in learning from other racial and religious groups.
L435: 
L436: This could signify that the multicultural narrative is "increasingly accessible" to younger cohorts of Singaporean residents who have gone through national education programmes, said IPS.
L437: Interest in understanding other cultures’ customs and practices had also grown slightly.
L438: 
L439: About four in 10 respondents (41.8 per cent) agreed or strongly agreed that they had an interest in understanding other racial groups' customs and practices, up from 38.3 per cent in 2018.
L440: 
L441: Likewise, 37.9 per cent of respondents were interested in learning about other religious beliefs and practices, compared to 33.9 per cent in 2018.
L442: Racial and religious minorities, as well as younger respondents, were more likely to be curious about different customs.
L443: 
L444: The survey results overall act as a "reality check" on the state of social cohesion, racial and religious harmony across Singapore, said Dr Puthucheary.
L445: 
L446: He added that the workplace was "increasingly important" for OnePeople.sg's work on social cohesion.
L447: "In other words, yes, things are improving in the workplace, but as things are improving more in all the other spaces, we have to pay more attention to what happens in the workplace.
L448: 
L449: "So the workplace becomes a relatively more significant area of focus."
L450: 
L451: In a response to the survey results, OnePeople.sg said that it was working to address divides that extend across generational, educational and socio-economic lines.
L452: The organisation had commenced a series of community dialogues in collaboration with educational institutions, ethnic and religious organisations to foster open and respectful exchanges.
L453: 
L454: This will allow participants of diverse backgrounds to better understand one another's perspectives and build meaningful connections, said OnePeople.sg.
L455: 
L456: It had also launched the Workplace Diversity Programme in partnership with IPS which had seen "positive results".
